profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a global macro strategy firm between the research lead and the publications/operations lead to align handoffs for a policy brief based on a new working paper on monetary-fiscal dynamics. The team is preparing materials for an external client roundtable two weeks away. The agenda is to confirm what goes into the 'pre-read,' which chart pack version will be used, how the empirical appendix and policy summary are split between the research and publishing workstreams, and what counts as the draft being 'ready for circulation.' The expected outcome is apparent agreement on deliverables, timeline, and ownership so the research note, slide deck, and appendix can move forward without further meetings.

members.name: Daniel Hsu
members.expertise: Macroeconomic modeling, policy analysis, empirical economic history
members.background: Daniel leads the firm's thematic research program and previously worked as an economist at a central bank before moving into private-sector macro strategy; he is used to circulating iterative internal drafts among senior stakeholders before publication formatting is complete.
members.private_state: He wants to preserve the nuance of the framework and get early intellectual buy-in from the chief economist and client-facing partners before the analysis is simplified too much; he is worried that the policy implications will be misread as partisan if the caveats and appendix context are stripped out.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pre-read' for senior stakeholders can be an analytically dense internal draft with provisional charts and caveats, as long as the core argument is visible.
The 'current deck' means the latest research-team working slides stored in the shared research folder, even if the publishing team has not yet mirrored them.
When a note is said to be 'ready for circulation,' that means ready for limited internal review by leadership, not external client distribution.
The appendix naturally includes methodological notes, robustness checks, and source annotations because those are part of making empirical claims safe to discuss.

If the policy summary says 'rebalance toward the consumption-and-wages loop,' readers will understand that this is a directional implication contingent on the model, not an immediate recommendation list.

members.name: Priya Raman
members.expertise: Research operations, executive communications, compliance-ready publication workflows
members.background: Priya manages how research outputs are packaged and cleared for clients; she came from an investor-relations communications team and is accustomed to tight version control, audience-specific summaries, and polished pre-reads that can be forwarded without context.
members.private_state: She wants to avoid a last-minute scramble or accidental circulation of unvetted policy language to clients; she is concerned about reputational risk if rough charts or methodological caveats appear inconsistent across the note and deck.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pre-read' is a polished, concise document suitable to be forwarded by executives, so anything called that should already be near-publication quality.
The 'current deck' means the latest approved slide file in the publications workspace with locked chart titles, numbering, and branding.
When a note is 'ready for circulation,' it means cleared for external client emailing after only light formatting checks.
The appendix for a client-facing brief should be limited to endnotes and source citations unless someone explicitly requests a separate technical supplement.
If the policy summary is included, it should translate the research into a short actionable takeaway without relying on readers to infer caveats from the full paper.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree to send a 'pre-read' before the client roundtable.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes the pre-read is an internal analytical draft for leadership review, potentially 8-10 pages with provisional framing, technical caveats, and draft charts.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes the pre-read is a polished executive summary, around 2-3 pages, clean enough to be forwarded to clients or board-level contacts.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In professional research settings, 'pre-read' is a common coordination term that often shifts by audience; because both think they are discussing an obvious preparation artifact, neither pauses to specify intended recipients or polish level.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the note and appendix should match the 'current deck.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the research team's Monday slide deck in the research drive that includes an updated 1980 regime-shift chart and two backup slides on loop-flow decomposition.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the publications team's Friday-approved deck in the communications workspace that still uses the older inflation trend chart and excludes backup slides.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both files are routinely called 'the current deck,' and because version control is normally implicit within each workstream, each assumes the other is anchored to the same artifact without needing the filename or date stated.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree on having the draft 'ready for circulation' by next Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the draft is analytically stable enough to circulate internally to the chief economist and regional strategy heads for comments, even if charts and wording may still change.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the document is effectively final for external distribution, with compliance-safe language, locked exhibits, and only formatting edits remaining.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase sounds like a routine deadline label rather than a substantive decision, and each person's criterion is normal in their own function, so the different threshold for 'ready' stays invisible.

misalignment_points.topic: What is included in the appendix
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that research will 'handle the appendix' while publications focuses on the summary note.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the appendix includes methods, robustness tests, alternative periodization around 1980, chart notes, and the loop-flow variable construction so skeptical readers can inspect the logic.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the appendix is only a short citation/endnote section attached to the brief, while any heavy methodology would be a separate technical paper not part of this deliverable.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Appendix scope is usually inherited from prior publication norms rather than redefined in coordination meetings, and both roles can sincerely say 'appendix' while imagining different packaging boundaries.

turns.inner_thought: I want to get this in front of the chief economist and the regional strategy heads early enough that they react to the actual framework, not a stripped-down version. For me the pre-read is the research team's working draft: dense enough to show the loop logic, caveats, and provisional charts, even if publications hasn't polished it yet. If we wait for everything to look publication-perfect, we'll lose the chance for substantive feedback.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. I mainly want to line up the handoff for the policy brief and make sure the pre-read goes out ahead of the roundtable next week so people have enough context.

turns.inner_thought: Good, same timing I had in mind. I need to pin down the package so we don't end up with a rough internal-style document being passed around as if it's client-ready. Pre-read to me means something clean and concise that an executive could forward without apology. I also need to know which current deck we're anchoring to, and I assume appendix means the standard back matter unless someone asks for a separate technical supplement.
turns.utterance: That timing works. What I need most is clarity on what sits in the summary note, what research is putting into the appendix, and which current deck we're matching to so the package moves cleanly.

turns.inner_thought: Research should definitely own the appendix. It needs the methods, robustness tables, alternative dating around the 1980 break, and the variable construction for the two loop flows. Otherwise the core claims look too bare and people will overread the policy angle. I'll also send the framing on the two loops and the regime-shift material so leadership can see the logic chain.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. Research will handle the appendix, and I'll send over the latest framing on the two loop flows along with the regime-shift material and the supporting notes.

turns.inner_thought: Perfect. If research handles the appendix, my team can stay focused on a crisp client-facing summary. I really just need the citations, source checks, and the supporting back matter by Tuesday so the brief can go through layout cleanly. If Daniel wants more technical detail later, that should be a separate piece, but I don't need to raise that now since we're aligned on research owning the appendix.
turns.utterance: Great, that actually helps a lot. If research is handling the appendix, we can keep the summary tight on our side, and I really just need the citations and supporting back matter by Tuesday.

turns.inner_thought: I should anchor us to the current deck the research team has been updating since Monday. The revised 1980 transition chart is much better, and the backup decomposition slides matter because they show why the monetary story alone is incomplete. If the note diverges from those slides, people will get mixed signals.
turns.utterance: Good. And I do want the note and appendix to stay aligned with the current deck, especially around the updated 1980 transition material and the backup decomposition work.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, absolutely—the current deck in the publications folder is the only safe anchor if we want stable titles, numbering, and branded exhibits. I assume that's what he means. If we start pulling in research backups or swapped charts late in the process, the note and deck can drift and we'll have a mess in review.
turns.utterance: Agreed. We'll format the narrative around the current deck already in the publication folder so the chart numbering and titles stay stable.

turns.inner_thought: As long as the pre-read preserves the analytical nuance, I'm fine. Leadership needs to see that this isn't just a money-supply story; the fiscal balance channel matters, and the caveats need to travel with the claim so it doesn't look like we're making a blunt policy statement. I don't need to spell all that out here because of course a pre-read should do that.
turns.utterance: On the pre-read, my only strong preference is that it preserves enough technical nuance for people to see why money supply alone isn't sufficient without the fiscal balance argument.

turns.inner_thought: That's fine—I can make the pre-read polished and concise while still signaling the core argument. First page should clearly state the takeaway, and the rest can support it without becoming a long draft. If it's easy to forward, executives will actually use it, which is the whole point.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I'll make sure the pre-read is concise and easy to forward, with the main takeaway visible on the first page.

turns.inner_thought: Next Thursday should be enough to get the draft analytically stable for internal leadership review. I specifically want reactions from the chief economist and strategy heads before the wording gets flattened by publication constraints. 'Ready for circulation' means ready for that internal review pass, not final-final.
turns.utterance: Then let's aim to have the full draft ready for circulation by next Thursday so the chief economist and strategy heads can react before wording gets locked.

turns.inner_thought: Next Thursday works if ready for circulation means effectively final and safe for external distribution after compliance language and formatting checks. If we hit that milestone, my team can close the last details and we won't be scrambling right before the roundtable.
turns.utterance: Next Thursday works for ready for circulation. That should give us enough room on our side to finish compliance language and the final formatting in time for external distribution.

turns.inner_thought: I'll send the appendix draft once the team closes the robustness notes on the historical break. That bundle will include the revised research charts and the policy framing, with the methods and supporting material attached. The policy language has to stay tied to the caveats or it can be misread as partisan, but once they see the full package it should be fine.
turns.utterance: Perfect. I'll send over the draft appendix, the revised charts, and the policy framing as soon as the team finishes the robustness notes on the historical break.

turns.inner_thought: Good—once his appendix materials arrive, we'll build the pre-read package off the current deck and the summary note in the publications workflow. I assume those appendix materials are the usual back matter, and then we can keep everything polished and controlled. Sounds like we have what we need without another meeting.
turns.utterance: Sounds good. Then we'll prepare the pre-read package from the current deck and the summary note once your appendix materials come through.
